<x_0.0254><y_0.1156>WILLIAMSBURG, a town of North America, in
Virginia, and formerly capital of that fate. It is situated
between two creeks; one falling into James, and the other
into York River. The distance of each landing place is
about a mile from the town, which, with the disadvantage
of not being able to bring up large veffels, and the want of
enterprife in the inhabitants, has occationed its decay. Here
is a college, defigned for the education of the Indians, but
which, on account of their avertion to learning, never an-
fwered the purpose. It is 60 miles east of Richmond. W.
Long. 76. 30. N. Lat. 37. 10.<x_0.9072><y_0.2648><class_Text>

<x_0.0234><y_0.2625>WILLIAMSTADT, a fea-port town of Holland. It
is a handfome frong place, and the harbour is well frequent-
ed. It was built by William prince of Orange in 1585;
and in 1732 belonged to the fladtholder of Frieland. The
river near which it is built is called _Butterflict_ or _Holland_
_Disp_; and is one of the bulwarks of the Dutch on the fide
of Brabant, where they always keep a garrifon. This place
made a gallant defence in 1793 against the French, who
were obliged to raife the flege. It is 15 miles north-eaft of
Bergen-op-Zoom, and 12 fourth-weft of Dort. E. Long.
4. 30. N. Lat. 51. 39.<x_0.9082><y_0.4117><class_Text>

<x_0.0215><y_0.4094>WILLIS (Dr Thomas), a celebrated Engliith phyfician,
was born at Great Bodwin, in Wiltfhire, in 1621, and
fluidied at Chrift-church college, Oxford. When that city
was garrisoned for the king, he, among other ferholars, bore
arms for his Majcity, and devoted his leifure hours to the
fludy of phyfic. The garrifon of Oxford at length furren-
dering to the parliament, he applied himself to the practice
of his profeffion; and foon rendered himself famous by his
care and fill. He appropriated a room as an oratory for
divine service according to the church of England, whither
moft of the loyalitts in Oxford daily reforted. In 1660, he
became Sedleian profeeffor of natural philosophy, and the
fame year took the degree of doctor of phyfic. In 1664,
he dificovered the famous medicinal iprinz at Altropp, near
Brackley. He was one of the first members of the Royal
Society, and foon made his name illustrious by his excellent
writings. In 1666, after the fire of London, he removed
to Weltminfter; and his practice became greater than that
of any of the phyficians his contemporaries. Soon after
his feettlement in London, his only ton Thomas falling into
a confumption, he fent him to Montpelier in France for the
recovery of his health; and it proved fuccefstul. His wife
alfo labouring under the fame diforder, he offered to leave
the town; but file, not suffering him to neglect the means
of providing for his family, died in 1670. He died at his
houte in St Martin's in 1675, and was buried near her in
Weltminfter-abbey. Dr Willis was extremely modell and
unambitious, and refufed the honogr of knighthood. He
was remarkably pious: As he rofe early in the morning,
that he might be prefent at divine service, which he conflant-
ly frequented before he vifted his patients, he procured
prayers to be read beyond the accultomed times while he
lived; and at his death fettled a flipend of 20l. per annum
to continue them. He was a liberal benefactor to the poor
wherever he came, having from his early practice allotted
part of his profits to charitable ufes. He was exact and regular in all his hours: and though his table was the report
of molt of the great men of London, yet he was remark-<x_0.9043><y_0.9203><class_Text>
